cells.tense: You are here with the pen, in the middle of the work itself.
cells.ask: Show the unfinished version to one person this week — the part that isn't polished yet — and let their response reach you.
cells.core:
What you're doing is small and daily, and you've stopped needing it to be more than that. A spark doesn't announce itself; it just keeps lighting, and yours has settled into that — repeated, unglamorous, actually working. You're not performing the practice for anyone. That's why it's holding.

The healthy version is unspectacular: you show up to the same small thing whether or not it's going anywhere yet. The bend is that nobody sees the middle of it, the part still forming. Let one person in on the unfinished version. A light doesn't need an audience, but you might be surprised what happens when it has one.
cells.sheetLine: You keep the small practice lit, and it's working.
cells.verb: letting a spark catch before it knows what it's for
cells.place: a small light kept lit by repetition, away from anyone watching

cells.tense: You're already standing at a finished version, bracing for a future that can't be written in yet.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you're refining and stop at the version that exists today — no next improvement, no private deadline, just done for now.
cells.core:
You're working toward a version of this that doesn't exist yet. Every repetition is pointed at the day it finally arrives — the day you'll be good enough, ready enough, finished. So the practice stops being practice and becomes a rehearsal for a life that keeps receding.

Done properly, this is plain practice: you're in the middle of something unfinished, and that's fine. The forward lean is what's bending it. You're pouring energy into a version of you that hasn't happened, and the gap keeps widening. Do today's piece and let it be enough as it is. The finish line will still be there tomorrow. What you'd actually gain is the hours you keep spending ahead of yourself.
cells.sheetLine: You're rehearsing a finished version instead of just practicing.

cells.tense: You're still standing at a door that's already behind you, waiting to feel ready.
cells.ask: Tell one person about a practice you've let go quiet — just the fact of it, nothing more — and listen to what they say back.
cells.core:
The doing has gone quiet. You know how to keep something lit by attention, and the attention isn't landing anywhere. Maybe it dried up. Maybe life took the room for it. Either way the habit stopped, and you're waiting for the feeling to return before you start again.

In working order this is simple: a thing you do on ordinary days, without checking whether it's going anywhere. What's missing is the repeat itself, not the capacity for it. You don't have to push yourself back into the same shape, and the last attempt doesn't owe you a verdict. Do it in company instead — one person, one sentence about something you've let drop. A spark doesn't need forcing. It needs something to catch on.
cells.sheetLine: You've stopped the small daily thing and you're waiting to feel ready.

cells.tense: You're already in the middle of the work, but you'd call it something else.
cells.ask: Name one habit you do without noticing — the one you wouldn't call a practice — and say it out loud as something you've built.
cells.core:
Something in you is already repeating itself into shape — the thing you do without noticing, the small returns you call anything but practice. It's been running in the background of your days, and it's yours. The name just hasn't caught up with the doing.

A kept practice looks like this from the inside: you can point at it and say you made it. The credit keeps going elsewhere — to luck, to personality, to just how you are. Those aren't the source. Say it once, out loud, that you built this, and notice what shifts when the quiet thing gets named as yours.
